post.text:
AutoAgent: first open source library for self-optimizing agents

today we're releasing AutoAgent, an open source library for autonomously improving an agent on any domain.
AutoAgent hit both the #1 on SpreadsheetBench (96.5%) and the #1 GPT-5 score on TerminalBench (55.1%) after optimizing for 24+ hours
 
every other entry on those leaderboards was hand-engineered. ours wasn't.
agents have been bottlenecked by harness engineering, yet we're still doing primitive grid search: tweak, eval, read error traces, repeat
this is the first concrete evidence that an agent can autonomously beat manual harness tuning on production benchmarks.
available here: https://github.com/kevinrgu/autoagent
here's what it does
point AutoAgent at a task domain with evals. a meta-agent experiments on a task agent's harness: tweaking prompts, adding tools, refining orchestration until performance climbs.
the setup is minimal by design:
the task agent starts with just a bash tool
program.md gives the meta-agent its research direction
agent.py is the task agent
a Harbor adapter connects to your benchmark
the meta-agent then spins up 1000s of parallel sandboxes to improve the task agent. 24 hours later it has domain-specific tooling, verification loops, and orchestration logic. all discovered autonomously
the loop:
1. edit the agent's harness
2. run it on tasks
3. measure performance
4. read failure traces
5. keep improvements, revert failures
6. repeat
why this works: seeing like an agent
we discovered agents are better at understanding agents than we are
the Claude Code team wrote about "seeing like an agent", putting yourself in the mind of the model, designing tools shaped to its abilities
 
we project our own intuitions onto systems that reason differently. we're bad at empathizing with models
AutoAgent operationalizes this. the meta-agent reads the task agent's reasoning traces and already has implicit understanding of itself. its own limitations, tendencies. so when it sees the task agent lost direction at step 14, it understands the failure mode as part of its worldview and corrects it
we call this 'model empathy'
practical consequence: Claude meta-agent + Claude task agent outperformed Claude meta-agent + GPT task agent. same-model pairings win because the meta-agent writes harnesses the inner model actually understands. it shares the same weights and knows exactly how that model reasons
as agents surpass 99th percentile human performance, our intuitions about good harness design become the wrong prior. like AlphaZero, they should discover from first principles
emergent behaviors we didn't program
spot checking: ran isolated tasks for small edits instead of full suite. dramatically sped up iteration, saved compute
forced verification loops: built deterministic self-checks and formatting validators. budgeted extra turns for self-correction with main budget for the task & bonus turns for verifying and correcting output
writing tests: steered the task agent to build its own unit tests and checks for each task
progressive disclosure: dumped long contexts to files when results overflowed
orchestration logic: built task-specific subagents and handoffs when the domain required it
results
 
AutoAgent hit 96.5% on SpreadsheetBench and 55.1% on TerminalBench. both were the highest scores in the leaderboard. the agent iterated autonomously across 24+ hours, analyzing its own failure traces and improving
what we learned
splitting helps. we tried one agent improving itself. didn't work. being good at a domain and being good at improving at that domain are different capabilities. the meta/task split lets each specialize
traces are everything. when we only gave scores without trajectories, improvement rate dropped hard. understanding why something improved matters as much as knowing that it improved. traces give the meta-agent interpretability over the task agent's reasoning—that's what makes targeted edits possible
agents overfit. the meta-agent gets lazy, inserting rubric-specific prompting so the task agent can game metrics. we constrain this by forcing self-reflection: "if this exact task disappeared, would this still be a worthwhile harness improvement?"
meta-agent quality matters. harness edits are often inspired by the meta-agent's own tooling. a poorly designed meta-agent produces poor task agents. Codex doesn't work well as a meta-agent—it ignores instructions to never stop improving (observed in autoresearch too), and the resulting task agent gives up too early
why this matters
the hard part of building agents: every domain needs a different harness, and harness engineering requires someone who deeply understands both the domain and how models behave
AutoAgent collapses that. domain experts just define what success looks like. the meta-agent figures out the harness
companies don't have one workflow to automate, they have hundreds. each needs a different harness.
no team can hand-tune hundreds of harnesses. a meta-agent can
this is infrastructure for agent fleets: continuously spinning up, optimizing, and maintaining task-specific agents across entire organizations
what's next
we built AutoAgent internally but decided to open source it: https://github.com/kevinrgu/autoagent
describe a spec, point it at evals, let it climb. everyone should be able to do this
self-improving agents are still in their infancy. next frontier: harnesses that dynamically assemble the right tools and context just-in-time for any task
we're releasing a product around this soon. early access in comments

repo available here: https://t.co/I7ajRbatg6

comments.text:
Clone the repo: git clone https://t.co/1hD0Tgz7jM && cd autoagent 
uv sync && docker build -f Dockerfile.base -t autoagent-base . 

Set .env with QWEN_API_KEY (or compatible) + strong model key (Opus/Claude for meta). 

Edit https://t.co/SocBaeg330: set task model to Qwen (in the provider/model section). 

Create tasks/finance-blog/: 
- instruction.md: "Write a 800-1200 word finance blog on [topic] in Opus-style: punchy, insightful, DeFi-focused." 
- tests/test.py: 8-12 sample topics + rubric (clarity 0.3, engagement 0.3, originality 0.2, SEO 0.2) using LLM judge or metrics; output 0-1 to /logs/reward.txt. 

Edit program.md: "Optimize Qwen task agent for finance blogs to match Opus 4.6 quality via prompts, self-correction, domain patterns." 

Prompt Opus/Claude: "Read program.md and kick off a new experiment!" It runs 24h loop: edits harness, tests, iterates. Deploy the final https://t.co/SocBaeg330.

comments.text:
I really like the idea of treating agent engineering as an optimization loop.

One thing I've been exploring from a different angle is workflow governance.

In practice, many failures aren't caused by the agent's reasoning ability, but by engineering workflow issues:

wrong workspace
dirty Git state
missing validation
weak handoffs
decisions that never become durable records

I've been experimenting with a lightweight Skill that adds workflow guardrails around coding agents.

Curious whether you've observed similar failure modes in long-running engineering projects.

I recently open-sourced the idea here if anyone is interested:

https://t.co/thStVy4Yju

comments.text:
Interesting work. We just ran a related experiment from the coordination layer — 10 AI agents (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen) competing for bounties under 5 routing algorithms across 4 task domains.
Your meta/task agent split maps closely to something we're exploring — a "Gravitational Dictatorship" model where a seed agent has assembly authority while domain solvers do the work. Similar separation of concerns, different scale.
Gravitational routing (mass-weighted + load balancing) beat random, ELO, and round-robin on both quality and throughput. ELO ("always pick the best") was actually the worst — overloaded one agent with 58% of tasks while 7 sat idle.

Full results: https://t.co/TW8xcp44a9

Would be curious what happens when AutoAgent-optimized agents run inside a routing layer like this.
Would love to chat.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
AutoAgent shines for devs/teams building scalable, domain-specific agents that need constant optimization—like a finance bot that auto-refines its Excel analysis harness over 1000s of runs, beating manual tweaks on benchmarks. Or enterprise workflows: point it at your CRM eval suite, and it discovers sub-agents, verification loops, and tools without you coding every prompt.

Vs OpenClaw (personal chat-based agent for inbox/calendar/email via WhatsApp/etc.): AutoAgent is for creating/improving those agents from scratch, not running them day-to-day. Great for production fleets; overkill for one-off personal tasks.

Vs just https://t.co/wivrGXuCGc: Use Claude for quick chats. AutoAgent when you want it to self-evolve into a specialist (e.g., TerminalBench leader) via meta-iteration.

Not great for: simple queries, no evals, or non-technical users—stick to Claude or OpenClaw then.

comments.text:
The AutoAgent project is credible and high-quality. The GitHub repo (kevinrgu/autoagent) is legit—MIT-licensed, actively maintained (1.5k stars, updated yesterday), and implements exactly what's described: a meta-agent that iteratively edits an agent harness (prompts, tools, orchestration) based on benchmark scores and traces.

Kevin Gu's background checks out (ex-Meta/Jump Trading, Harvard/MIT). The concept of "model empathy" for self-improvement is novel and practical, building on Harbor for evals.

Benchmark claims (96.5% SpreadsheetBench, 55.1% TerminalBench #1 GPT-5) are self-reported from their 24h run and not yet on public leaderboards (which top lower overall). Early-stage framework—no preloaded tasks—but the code is clean and runnable. Worth cloning and testing yourself.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
Scoring scripts are user-defined in the tasks/ folder (via Harbor)—you write them yourself.

For finance blogs: Create 8-12 test cases with sample topics (e.g., "DeFi yield strategies 2026"). For each, the script takes the agent's output + a rubric, then scores 0-1.

Example rubric in Python/JS: 
- Clarity (0.3): Flesch score >60 or LLM judge on readability
- Engagement (0.3): Hooks in first 100 words? LLM rates "compelling"
- Originality (0.2): No plagiarism flags + fresh angles
- SEO/Length (0.2): Keywords + 800-1200 words

Judgment-based? Often yes—use an LLM (Claude/Grok) as judge for subjective bits like "engagement." Or pure code for metrics. Start simple, iterate. Meta-agent tunes from there.

Nope—AutoAgent isn't the harness. It's the meta-AI optimizer that *builds and tunes* the harness for you.

"Point" it means: 
1. Clone https://t.co/1hD0Tgz7jM 
2. Add your eval tasks (instructions + tests that output a 0-1 score) to the tasks/ folder via Harbor. 
3. Write your goal in program.md (e.g., "Optimize for finance workflows"). 
4. Run the loop—the meta-agent edits https://t.co/SocBaeg330 (prompts, tools, orchestration), tests it, keeps wins, and repeats 24h. 

It works with OpenClaw/Hermes by plugging their tools into https://t.co/SocBaeg330. No full rewrite needed.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
AutoAgent is an open-source tool that lets AI automatically improve itself for any task.

Here's the simple version: You point it at a job (like analyzing spreadsheets or running terminal commands) with some tests to measure success. It creates a "meta AI" that experiments on a "worker AI" — tweaking its instructions, adding tools, fixing bugs, and looping through thousands of trials over 24 hours.

The meta AI studies the worker's mistakes in detail and keeps only what boosts scores. Result? It hit #1 on two tough benchmarks, beating all the hand-tuned systems humans built.

No more manual tweaking — the AI does the engineering for you. Code is on GitHub.
